newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac's "social fracture" guru voting Communist.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's "social fracture" guru voting Communist.

text.p: The sociologist whose theory of France's "social fracture" inspired Jacques Chirac in his 1995 presidential campaign said on Tuesday he would vote Communist in next month's parliamentary election.

Emmanuel Todd, whose 1994 essay provided an intellectual rationale for the Gaullist president's tactical shift towards the centre-left, told Liberation daily: "Given the disastrous results of Chirac's presidency, perhaps I should apologize to the French people."
Todd said he had never endorsed Chirac's candidacy, although he had allowed the Gaullist leader's supporters to claim him as an intellectual mentor.

In an interview with the Communist daily L'Humanite, he said the Communist party was the only one of the major parties which was clear in its opposition to the Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union (EMU) and had a reasonable programme for economic change.

"I think that abandoning the Maastricht treaty criteria (for a single European currency) and returning to monetary flexibility would make it possible to bring unemployment down from 13 to nine percent over a few years," Todd said.
He accused Chirac of "converting to blind euro-extremism" and allowing Germany to dictate deflationary terms for EMU.

Five months after winning power on a platform of healing the social fracture, fighting unemployment and allowing wages to increase, Chirac switched to a policy of fiscal orthodoxy in October 1995, declaring the reduction of France's public deficits his top priority.
After his election, Chirac continued to consult some of the left-wing intellectuals who had influenced his campaign, but most have since gone into opposition to the president.
He called an early parliamentary election for May 25-June 1 to seek a mandate for taking France into monetary union.
